strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: retaining information across long horizons in offline partially observable reinforcement learning without expanding the transformer’s attention window.

The strongest evidence is the T-Maze ablation in Table 3. After training on lengths up to 150, RATE achieves 0.90 ± 0.07 success at length 900, versus 0.61 ± 0.07 without MRV. This supports the proposed update mechanism’s usefulness for this task.

Evaluation spans visual and vector observations, discrete and continuous actions, and several memory tasks. The curriculum, memory-corruption, caching, and alternative-MRV experiments provide useful diagnostic evidence. Improvements on Breakout and Qbert are also substantial.

The manuscript provides a code link, dataset-construction descriptions, hyperparameter tables, and hardware information. Matching DT’s context to RATE’s effective training context is a useful experimental control.
weaknesses: Novelty and competitive positioning remain insufficiently established. RATE primarily combines DT, Recurrent Memory Transformer, Transformer-XL, and a conventional cross-attention update. Although component ablations are useful, the main memory-task comparisons predominantly use finite-window DT. Comparisons with standalone recurrent policies, established memory transformers, and state-space policies trained on the same offline data are needed to establish an advantage over competitive memory architectures.

The training description contains a consequential contradiction. Section 3 states that updated memory embeddings are detached, then says gradients flow through those embeddings to previous segments. Detachment blocks that path. The manuscript must specify exactly which tensors are detached, the backpropagation horizon, and how MRV receives its learning signal. Cache lengths and attention-mask construction also require clearer specification.

The ViZDoom information restrictions are not reconciled with return conditioning. Appendix A.1 says rewards are withheld because they reveal the pillar color, but Section 3 supplies return-to-go tokens updated by R_{t+1} = R_t - r_t. Consecutive tokens therefore reveal rewards under the stated procedure. Clarification and a control excluding this information channel are needed before attributing performance exclusively to long-term retention of the initial cue.

The MuJoCo comparison confounds architecture with inference strategy. Appendix C resets RATE’s target return to its maximum at every segment, while DT scores are taken from prior work. Without evaluating both methods with and without this reset, the reported improvements in all nine tasks cannot be cleanly attributed to recurrent memory.

Some reported interpretations conflict with the figures. Figure 5(b) shows randomized-memory success around 0.35–0.40 at long horizons, whereas Section 5 describes 0.50 and concludes that navigation remains intact. The plotted degradation could reflect broader policy disruption. Training-seed counts and uncertainty definitions are also unclear for Figure 5 and Table 3.

The parameter accounting omits part of the proposed architecture: the claimed increase of only embedding_dimension × memory_tokens excludes MRV’s learned attention projections. Table 7 reports shared, rounded parameter counts and training times for DT and RATE. Exact per-model counts and separate runtime measurements are needed to substantiate the efficiency comparison.
